question_html: Which of the following persons falls within the definition of 'promoter' under section 2(69) of the Companies Act, 2013?

options.A: A person in accordance with whose advice, directions, or instructions the Board of Directors of the company is accustomed to act, PROVIDED that such person is not acting merely in a professional capacity such as an attorney or a technical/functional expert
options.B: A chartered accountant engaged purely in a professional capacity to certify the company's financial statements, with no involvement in directing the company's affairs
options.C: A legal counsel retained purely in a professional capacity to draft the company's contracts, with no involvement in directing the company's affairs
options.D: A technical consultant engaged purely in a professional capacity to advise on plant machinery, with no involvement in directing the company's affairs

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) A person in accordance with whose advice, directions, or instructions the Board of Directors of the company is accustomed to act, PROVIDED that such person is not acting merely in a professional capacity such as an attorney or a technical/functional expert

Section 2(69) includes, among others, a person in accordance with whose advice, directions, or instructions the Board is accustomed to act - but expressly excludes a person acting merely in a professional capacity (such as an attorney, or a technical or functional expert).

question_html: Must a person necessarily be associated with the INITIAL formation of a company in order to be regarded as its 'promoter'?

options.A: Yes; only a person associated with the company's initial formation can ever be regarded as its promoter, and any later involvement is legally irrelevant to promoter status
options.B: No; one who subsequently helps to arrange the floating of the company's capital (or otherwise helps the company get going) will equally be regarded as a promoter, even without being associated with the company's initial formation
options.C: Yes, but only if that person is also named as a subscriber to the memorandum, this being an essential precondition for promoter status under section 2(69)
options.D: No; but only a person who advances share capital to the company (as opposed to merely arranging its floatation) can be regarded as a promoter

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No; one who subsequently helps to arrange the floating of the company's capital (or otherwise helps the company get going) will equally be regarded as a promoter, even without being associated with the company's initial formation

As illustrated in the Study Material, a promoter need not be associated with the initial formation of a company - one who subsequently helps arrange the floating of its capital, or otherwise helps keep the company going (other than in a purely professional capacity), is equally regarded as a promoter.

question_html: Under section 3(1), what is the minimum number of persons required to form (respectively) a public company, a private company, and a One Person Company?

options.A: Two (2) or more persons for a public company, seven (7) or more persons for a private company, and two (2) persons for a One Person Company
options.B: Five (5) or more persons for a public company, three (3) or more persons for a private company, and one (1) person for a One Person Company

question_html: Under Rule 3 of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014, who is eligible to incorporate a One Person Company?

options.A: Only a natural person, other than a minor, who is a resident Indian citizen - a non-resident Indian citizen is NOT eligible to incorporate an OPC

question_html: What is the purpose of the mandatory nominee provision for a One Person Company, and what must accompany the nominee's name in the memorandum?

options.A: The nominee ensures perpetual succession of the OPC's legal existence, becoming its member in the event of the subscriber's death or incapacity to contract; the memorandum must indicate the nominee's name along with his prior written consent in the requisite form
options.B: The nominee acts merely as an honorary title-holder with no legal consequence whatsoever, and no consent of any kind is required from him at the time of incorporation
options.C: The nominee becomes a joint member of the OPC alongside the subscriber from the very date of incorporation, and his consent is required only if he is a relative of the subscriber
options.D: The nominee is required only for tax-filing purposes and has no role in the event of the subscriber's death or incapacity to contract

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The nominee ensures perpetual succession of the OPC's legal existence, becoming its member in the event of the subscriber's death or incapacity to contract; the memorandum must indicate the nominee's name along with his prior written consent in the requisite form

The nominee provision safeguards the OPC's perpetual succession: the memorandum must name the nominee (who must otherwise satisfy the same eligibility criteria as an OPC member) along with his prior written consent, so that he becomes the member upon the subscriber's death or incapacity to contract.

question_html: Can a natural person be a member of more than one OPC at any point in time, or be a nominee of more than one OPC?

options.A: Yes; a natural person may simultaneously be a member of any number of OPCs, provided each OPC is engaged in a distinct line of business
options.B: No; a natural person shall not be a member of more than one OPC at any point in time, and shall not be a nominee of more than one OPC - and where a person becomes a member of a second OPC by virtue of being a nominee, he must meet this single-OPC criterion within 180 days
options.C: Yes; a natural person may be a member of up to two OPCs simultaneously, though he may be a nominee of only one OPC at a time
options.D: No; a natural person may never be a nominee of any OPC if he is already a member of one, with no grace period allowed to cure a resulting dual-membership situation

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No; a natural person shall not be a member of more than one OPC at any point in time, and shall not be a nominee of more than one OPC - and where a person becomes a member of a second OPC by virtue of being a nominee, he must meet this single-OPC criterion within 180 days

Rule 3(2) restricts a natural person to being a member of only one OPC at any time, and to being a nominee of only one OPC. Where he becomes a member of a second OPC purely by virtue of being its nominee (e.g., on the first OPC's sole member's death), he must bring himself into compliance with this single-OPC rule within 180 days.

question_html: Under section 3A, members of a company become severally liable for the company's debts (in addition to their ordinary joint liability) where which combination of conditions is satisfied?

options.A: The number of members is reduced below seven (for a public company) or two (for a private company), with several liability attaching immediately upon such reduction, regardless of how long the company thereafter continues to carry on business or whether any member was aware of the reduction
options.B: The company's paid-up share capital falls below the prescribed minimum threshold, regardless of the actual number of members remaining or the length of time the company continues to carry on business thereafter
options.C: The number of members is reduced below seven (for a public company) or two (for a private company), the company carries on business for MORE THAN SIX MONTHS with the reduced number of members, and the relevant member was cognizant (aware) of this fact while the business was so carried on
options.D: The company fails to hold its annual general meeting for two consecutive years, regardless of the number of members remaining or their awareness of any membership shortfall

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The number of members is reduced below seven (for a public company) or two (for a private company), the company carries on business for MORE THAN SIX MONTHS with the reduced number of members, and the relevant member was cognizant (aware) of this fact while the business was so carried on

Section 3A requires three cumulative conditions for several liability: (i) membership falls below the statutory minimum (7 for public, 2 for private), (ii) the company carries on business for more than six months with the reduced membership, and (iii) the person sought to be held liable was aware (cognizant) that the business was being carried on with such reduced membership.

question_html: Where the conditions of section 3A are satisfied, for what debts are the relevant members severally liable?

options.A: For the payment of the whole debts of the company contracted from the very date on which the membership was first reduced below the statutory minimum, including debts contracted during the initial six-month grace period
options.B: For the payment of only 50% of the debts contracted by the company after the six-month grace period has elapsed, this being a specific statutory apportionment under section 3A
options.C: For the payment of the whole debts of the company contracted at ANY time during its existence, whether before or after the membership reduction, so long as the member was aware of the reduction at some point
options.D: For the payment of the whole debts of the company contracted DURING THE PERIOD after the six months have elapsed (i.e., debts contracted while the company continued in default, after the six-month grace period) - not debts contracted before that point

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) For the payment of the whole debts of the company contracted DURING THE PERIOD after the six months have elapsed (i.e., debts contracted while the company continued in default, after the six-month grace period) - not debts contracted before that point

Several liability under section 3A attaches only to debts contracted by the company DURING the period after the six-month grace period has elapsed (i.e., after the company has continued for more than six months with reduced membership) - not to debts contracted earlier, including during that initial six-month window.

question_html: Under section 3A, is the several liability of the relevant members IN ADDITION TO, or INSTEAD OF, their ordinary joint liability as members for the company's debts?

options.A: In addition to; members are generally jointly liable for the company's debts, but where section 3A's conditions are satisfied, they SHALL ALSO be severally liable (and may be severally sued) for the specified debts
options.B: Instead of; once section 3A applies, the members' ordinary joint liability is entirely extinguished and replaced solely by several liability for the specified debts
options.C: Neither; section 3A liability is a wholly distinct statutory liability owed directly to the Registrar of Companies, unconnected to either joint or several liability to creditors
options.D: In addition to, but only up to a maximum aggregate liability across all members equal to the company's paid-up share capital at the time of the reduction

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) In addition to; members are generally jointly liable for the company's debts, but where section 3A's conditions are satisfied, they SHALL ALSO be severally liable (and may be severally sued) for the specified debts

Section 3A operates as an ADDITIONAL layer of liability: members remain jointly liable for the company's debts as usual, but where the section's conditions are met, they become severally liable (and may be severally sued) as well, specifically for debts contracted during the relevant post-six-month period.

question_html: Under the Companies Act, 2013, is the certificate of incorporation conclusive proof of EVERYTHING prior to incorporation being in order (such as the legality of the objects stated in the memorandum)?

options.A: Yes; the certificate of incorporation is, and always has been, conclusive proof of the legality of every matter preceding incorporation, including the legality of the company's stated objects
options.B: No; the certificate of incorporation carries no evidentiary value whatsoever, not even as evidence of the company's registration or separate legal existence
options.C: No; unlike the earlier position, the certificate of incorporation under the Companies Act, 2013 is NOT conclusive proof of everything prior to incorporation being in order (for example, it does not validate illegal objects stated in the objects clause) - though it remains evidence of the company's registration and separate legal existence
options.D: Yes, but only for a private company; for a public company, the certificate of incorporation remains conclusive proof of everything prior to incorporation being in order

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) No; unlike the earlier position, the certificate of incorporation under the Companies Act, 2013 is NOT conclusive proof of everything prior to incorporation being in order (for example, it does not validate illegal objects stated in the objects clause) - though it remains evidence of the company's registration and separate legal existence

Sub-sections (6) and (7) of section 7 signify that, under the 2013 Act, the certificate of incorporation is not conclusive proof of everything prior to incorporation being in order - for instance, if a company is registered with illegal objects, the certificate does not validate those illegal objects; the only remedy is winding up.

question_html: Where a section 8 company's licence is revoked, and the Central Government (acting through the Regional Director), being satisfied that it is essential in the public interest, directs that the company be wound up, what happens to its excess assets on winding up (after satisfaction of its debts and liabilities)?

options.A: The excess assets shall, in every case, be distributed equally among all the members of the company, as would occur on winding up of an ordinary limited company
options.B: The excess assets shall, in every case, escheat to the State Government of the State in which the company's registered office was situated, with no possibility of transfer to another section 8 company
options.C: The excess assets may be transferred to another company registered under section 8 and having similar objects (subject to conditions the Tribunal may impose), OR sold, with the proceeds credited to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Fund formed under section 224 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
options.D: The excess assets shall be transferred to the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund in every case, regardless of the nature of the section 8 company's original charitable objects

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The excess assets may be transferred to another company registered under section 8 and having similar objects (subject to conditions the Tribunal may impose), OR sold, with the proceeds credited to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Fund formed under section 224 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

Where a section 8 company is wound up following revocation of its licence, its excess assets (after settling debts/liabilities) may be transferred to another section 8 company with similar objects, subject to Tribunal-imposed conditions, or sold with the proceeds credited to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Fund - reflecting the policy that charitable surplus should not be distributed to members.

options.A: A liability clause, stating the extent to which members' liability is limited
options.B: A capital clause, stating the amount of share capital and its division into shares of fixed amount (applicable where the company has share capital)

options.B: Such an act is ultra vires and wholly void ab initio - it cannot be ratified even by the unanimous assent of the entire body of shareholders; the principle was established in Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche
options.C: Such an act is valid and binding on the company in all respects, provided the third party dealing with the company acted in good faith and without notice of the objects clause
options.D: Such an act is void only against dissenting shareholders, but remains fully binding and enforceable as between the company and shareholders who voted in favour of it

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Such an act is ultra vires and wholly void ab initio - it cannot be ratified even by the unanimous assent of the entire body of shareholders; the principle was established in Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche

An act beyond the objects clause (ultra vires the company) is void ab initio and incapable of ratification even by unanimous shareholder consent, because the company itself never had the capacity to do it. This foundational principle was laid down in Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche.

question_html: How does an act that is ultra vires the powers of the directors (but within the company's objects) differ, in legal consequence, from an act that is ultra vires the company itself?

options.A: Both categories of acts are equally void and incapable of ratification under any circumstances, with no legal distinction drawn between them
options.B: An act ultra vires the directors is void and unratifiable, whereas an act ultra vires the company itself can always be ratified by a simple majority of shareholders present at a general meeting
options.C: An act ultra vires the directors (but intra vires the company) can be ratified by the shareholders in a general meeting, provided it is not beyond the powers of the company as stated in the memorandum; an act ultra vires the company itself is void and can never be ratified, even by all shareholders
options.D: Both categories of acts are automatically valid and binding on the company the moment any single director purports to authorise them, without any requirement of shareholder ratification

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) An act ultra vires the directors (but intra vires the company) can be ratified by the shareholders in a general meeting, provided it is not beyond the powers of the company as stated in the memorandum; an act ultra vires the company itself is void and can never be ratified, even by all shareholders

The law distinguishes: acts ultra vires the company (beyond the memorandum's objects) are void and cannot be ratified by anyone, since the company lacked capacity. Acts merely ultra vires the directors or the articles (but within the company's objects as stated in the memorandum) CAN be ratified by the shareholders in general meeting, since the company itself had the capacity to do the act.

question_html: Which of the following statements correctly describes an aspect of the doctrine of ultra vires?

options.A: Every act done by a company that is not expressly and specifically enumerated word-for-word in the objects clause is automatically ultra vires, with no scope for any act to be treated as merely incidental
options.B: The doctrine of ultra vires exists solely to protect the company's directors from personal liability, and has no bearing on the interests of shareholders or creditors
options.C: An injunction to restrain an ultra vires act can only be sought by the Central Government, and is not available to any individual member of the company
options.D: An act that is incidental to, or consequential upon, the objects specified in the memorandum is not deemed ultra vires, even if it is not explicitly stated as a separate object

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) An act that is incidental to, or consequential upon, the objects specified in the memorandum is not deemed ultra vires, even if it is not explicitly stated as a separate object

The doctrine permits acts that are incidental to or consequential upon the stated objects (reasonably necessary for their fulfilment) - these are not ultra vires. The doctrine's purpose is to protect shareholders (so their investment is used only for stated objects) and creditors (so company funds/assets are not diverted). Any member may seek an injunction to restrain a proposed ultra vires act, and no suit for specific performance lies on an ultra vires transaction, even at the instance of an outsider.

question_html: Under section 5, what do the articles of association of a company contain, and what happens if a company does not expressly exclude or modify the applicable model regulations?

options.A: The articles contain the regulations for management of the company, matters prescribed to be included, and any additional matters the company considers necessary; if the applicable Table (F, G, H, I or J, as the case may be) is not expressly excluded or modified, it applies to the company as if it were contained in its duly registered articles

question_html: What is an 'entrenchment provision' in the articles of association, and how may it be included?

options.A: A provision that permits the articles to be altered by an ordinary resolution instead of a special resolution, thereby making alteration easier rather than more restrictive
options.B: A provision making specified article alterations subject to more restrictive conditions or procedures than a special resolution; it may be included either at the time of formation, or by an amendment agreed to by all members (for a private company) or by a special resolution (for a public company)
options.C: A provision that can only be included in the articles of a listed public company, and is statutorily barred for private companies and unlisted public companies altogether
options.D: A provision that automatically expires and ceases to have effect five years after the date of the company's incorporation, regardless of the members' wishes

Correct answer: (B) A provision making specified article alterations subject to more restrictive conditions or procedures than a special resolution; it may be included either at the time of formation, or by an amendment agreed to by all members (for a private company) or by a special resolution (for a public company)

Section 5(3)-(4) defines entrenchment as making specified provisions alterable only by conditions/procedures more restrictive than a special resolution. It may be included at formation, or later by an amendment agreed to by all members (private company) or by special resolution (public company).

question_html: When must a company give notice of entrenchment provisions in its articles to the Registrar, under section 5(5)?

options.A: Notice of entrenchment provisions is never required to be given to the Registrar under any circumstances, as entrenchment is treated as a purely internal matter of the company
options.B: Notice must be given to the Registrar only once every three years, on a rolling basis, irrespective of whether the entrenchment provisions were included at formation or by later amendment

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Where entrenchment provisions are included at the time of formation, notice is given at the time of filing the articles (via SPICe+ etc.); where they are included by amendment after formation, notice must be given to the Registrar in the prescribed form (Form MGT-14) within 30 days from the date the entrenchment provisions take effect

Section 5(5) requires the company to give notice to the Registrar of entrenchment provisions in the prescribed manner - at formation, this is done at the time of filing articles; where included by later amendment, notice must be filed with the Registrar (Form MGT-14) within 30 days from the date the entrenchment provisions take effect.

question_html: What is the doctrine of constructive notice as applied to a company's memorandum and articles, and which case illustrates it?

options.A: The doctrine holds that only the company's own officers and employees are deemed to have notice of the memorandum and articles, while outside persons dealing with the company are entirely exempt from any such notice
options.B: The doctrine holds that a person dealing with the company is bound only by whatever the company's managing director personally and orally informs him, irrespective of the contents of the memorandum and articles
options.C: The doctrine applies exclusively to listed public companies, and has no application whatsoever to private companies or unlisted public companies
options.D: Since the memorandum and articles are public documents open for inspection (registered with the Registrar under section 399), every person dealing with the company is deemed to have constructive notice of their contents, whether or not he has actually read them; illustrated in Ernest v Nicholls

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Since the memorandum and articles are public documents open for inspection (registered with the Registrar under section 399), every person dealing with the company is deemed to have constructive notice of their contents, whether or not he has actually read them; illustrated in Ernest v Nicholls

Because the memorandum and articles are public documents (registered with the Registrar and open to public inspection under section 399), the law presumes that every person dealing with the company has constructive notice of their contents - actual knowledge is irrelevant since the law imputes it regardless. This was illustrated in Ernest v Nicholls.

question_html: What is the doctrine of indoor management (the 'Turquand Rule'), and what is its underlying rationale?

options.A: Persons dealing with a company in good faith are entitled to presume that the internal procedural requirements of the company's own constitution (e.g., internal authorisations, resolutions) have been duly and regularly complied with, and are not bound to verify the internal proceedings; established in Royal British Bank v. Turquand, to protect outsiders from a company later denying liability by pointing to its own internal irregularities
options.B: The doctrine requires every outsider dealing with a company to personally inspect and verify all internal board resolutions and internal management proceedings before entering into any transaction, failing which the transaction is automatically void
options.C: The doctrine holds that a company is never bound by any act of its directors or officers unless that act is separately ratified by all shareholders in a general meeting held specifically for that purpose
options.D: The doctrine applies only to transactions involving the sale of immovable property by a company, and has no application to any other type of company transaction

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Persons dealing with a company in good faith are entitled to presume that the internal procedural requirements of the company's own constitution (e.g., internal authorisations, resolutions) have been duly and regularly complied with, and are not bound to verify the internal proceedings; established in Royal British Bank v. Turquand, to protect outsiders from a company later denying liability by pointing to its own internal irregularities

The doctrine of indoor management (Royal British Bank v. Turquand) holds that outsiders dealing with a company in good faith may presume that the company's own internal requirements/procedures have been duly complied with - they need not inquire into the regularity of internal proceedings. This protects outsiders from a company escaping liability merely by showing that its own internal formalities were not observed, and operates as an exception to (or limitation on) the doctrine of constructive notice.

question_html: In which of the following situations would the doctrine of indoor management NOT protect an outsider dealing with a company?

options.A: Where the transaction was authorised by a person who, unknown to the outsider, held an internal management position within the company at the relevant time, and the outsider dealt with him in the ordinary course of business
options.B: Where the outsider had actual knowledge of the internal irregularity, or where the circumstances surrounding the transaction were suspicious enough that a reasonable person would have made further inquiry
options.C: Where the document relied upon by the outsider was genuinely signed and issued by a duly authorised officer of the company in the ordinary course of its business
options.D: Where the outsider dealing with the company was a first-time customer of the company, having had no prior dealings with it whatsoever

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Where the outsider had actual knowledge of the internal irregularity, or where the circumstances surrounding the transaction were suspicious enough that a reasonable person would have made further inquiry

The recognised exceptions to indoor management include: (i) actual knowledge of irregularity, (ii) negligence, including where suspicious circumstances ought to have put the outsider on inquiry, (iii) forgery (a forged document never binds the company at all - there is no valid document to presume regularity of), (iv) where the question is about the very existence of an agency, and (v) where an act requires a precondition that goes to the company's own capacity (ultra vires the company itself). Being a first-time customer, standing alone, is not among the recognised exceptions.

question_html: What does section 6 provide regarding the relationship between the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and a company's memorandum, articles, agreements, and resolutions?

options.A: The memorandum and articles of a company always override the provisions of the Act, since they represent the company's own privately negotiated internal constitution
options.B: Section 6 applies only to agreements and resolutions passed after the commencement of the Act, and has no retrospective application to agreements or resolutions passed before its commencement
options.C: Save as otherwise expressly provided in the Act, the provisions of the Act override anything to the contrary contained in the memorandum, articles, any agreement executed, or any resolution passed by the company (whether registered, executed or passed before or after the commencement of the Act), and any such contrary provision is void to that extent
options.D: Section 6 permits a company's articles to override any provision of the Act, provided the articles were registered with the Registrar prior to the relevant agreement or resolution being executed or passed

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Save as otherwise expressly provided in the Act, the provisions of the Act override anything to the contrary contained in the memorandum, articles, any agreement executed, or any resolution passed by the company (whether registered, executed or passed before or after the commencement of the Act), and any such contrary provision is void to that extent

Section 6 establishes the primacy of the Act: save as otherwise expressly provided, the Act's provisions have effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the memorandum, articles, any agreement, or any resolution (whether made before or after the Act's commencement), and any repugnant provision is void to that extent. An example of an express saving is section 47's proviso making the articles override section 47 itself in specified circumstances for private companies.

options.A: Wood v Odessa Waterworks Co
options.B: Rayfield v Hands
options.C: Browne v La Trinidad
options.D: Borland's Trustee v Steel Bros & Co Ltd

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Borland's Trustee v Steel Bros & Co Ltd

Section 10(1) gives the memorandum and articles the effect of a contract binding the company and its members. Borland's Trustee v Steel Bros & Co Ltd illustrates members being bound to the company. Wood v Odessa Waterworks Co illustrates the company being bound to members. Rayfield v Hands illustrates members being bound to members (in certain circumstances). Browne v La Trinidad illustrates that no outsider can enforce the articles against the company.

question_html: What did Browne v La Trinidad establish regarding the enforceability of a company's articles by an outsider (a person who is not a member)?

options.A: No article can constitute a contract between the company and a third person (an outsider); an outsider cannot sue the company to enforce the articles, even where the articles purport to confer a benefit or right on him
options.B: An outsider may always sue the company to enforce any provision of the articles, provided he can show that the provision was inserted specifically for his benefit
options.C: The articles bind the company to outsiders in exactly the same manner and to the same extent as they bind the company to its own members
options.D: An outsider may enforce the articles against the company only if he subsequently becomes a creditor of the company by lending it money

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No article can constitute a contract between the company and a third person (an outsider); an outsider cannot sue the company to enforce the articles, even where the articles purport to confer a benefit or right on him

Browne v La Trinidad established that the articles constitute a contract only between the company and its members (and among members inter se, in certain respects) - they do not create enforceable rights in favour of outsiders (non-members), even where a particular article purports to benefit such a person.

question_html: Under section 13, whose approval is generally required for a company to change its name, and what is the effect of the fresh certificate of incorporation issued on such change?

options.A: No governmental approval is required at all for a change of name - a special resolution of the members alone is sufficient to complete and effect the change
options.B: The approval of the Central Government (delegated to the Registrar of Companies) is required, except where the change is merely the addition or deletion of the word 'Private' consequent to conversion; a fresh certificate of incorporation is issued, and the change of name is effective and complete only from the date of that certificate
options.C: The approval of the shareholders alone, by an ordinary resolution, is both necessary and sufficient, with the Registrar having a purely ministerial role of recording the change without power to withhold it
options.D: The approval of the National Company Law Tribunal is mandatorily required for every change of name, regardless of the nature or reason for the change

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The approval of the Central Government (delegated to the Registrar of Companies) is required, except where the change is merely the addition or deletion of the word 'Private' consequent to conversion; a fresh certificate of incorporation is issued, and the change of name is effective and complete only from the date of that certificate

Section 13(2)/(3) requires a special resolution plus approval of the Central Government (powers delegated to the Registrar), except for the addition/deletion of 'Private' upon conversion. On approval, a fresh certificate of incorporation is issued, and the name change takes effect only from the date of that fresh certificate - not from the date of the special resolution.

question_html: What is required for a company to shift its registered office from one State to another?

options.A: An ordinary resolution of the members is sufficient on its own, with no requirement for any governmental approval or advertisement of the proposed shift
options.B: The written consent of the company's bankers alone is sufficient, since an inter-State shift of registered office is treated purely as a banking and taxation formality
options.C: A special resolution of the members, followed by the approval of the Central Government (powers delegated to the Regional Director), applied for in the prescribed form (Form INC-23) along with the prescribed documents and advertisement (Form INC-26); on approval, a fresh certificate of incorporation is issued by the Registrar of the new State
options.D: A resolution of the Board of Directors alone is sufficient, since the registered office is treated as a matter of day-to-day management rather than a matter requiring shareholder or governmental approval

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) A special resolution of the members, followed by the approval of the Central Government (powers delegated to the Regional Director), applied for in the prescribed form (Form INC-23) along with the prescribed documents and advertisement (Form INC-26); on approval, a fresh certificate of incorporation is issued by the Registrar of the new State

An inter-State shift of registered office requires a special resolution, Central Government approval (delegated to the Regional Director) via Form INC-23 with prescribed documents, advertisement in Form INC-26, and the application must be disposed of within 60 days. On approval, the Registrar of the new State issues a fresh certificate of incorporation.

question_html: Under section 16, within what period must a trademark proprietor apply for rectification of a company's name that too nearly resembles his registered trademark?

options.A: Within thirty days of the incorporation of the company, failing which the trademark proprietor permanently loses the right to seek rectification
options.B: Within one year of the incorporation of the company, extendable at the sole discretion of the Registrar for a further period of one year only
options.C: There is no time limit for a trademark proprietor to apply for rectification under section 16, and an application may be made at any time
options.D: Within three years of the incorporation, registration, or change of name of the company (as the case may be)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Within three years of the incorporation, registration, or change of name of the company (as the case may be)

Section 16 allows the Central Government (delegated to Regional Director) to direct a company to change a name that is identical with, or too nearly resembles, an existing company's name or a registered trademark. Where the application is by a trademark proprietor, it must be made within three years of the company's incorporation, registration of name, or change of name. On direction, the company must comply within 3 months by ordinary resolution and notify the Registrar within 15 days, failing which the Central Government itself allots a new name.

question_html: Under section 14, what additional requirement applies where a public company alters its articles so as to convert itself into a private company?

options.A: Such alteration (conversion into a private company) shall not take effect except with the approval of the Central Government (delegated to the Regional Director), applied for within 60 days of the special resolution, along with the prescribed documents
options.B: No additional requirement applies at all - a special resolution of the members alone is fully sufficient to effect the conversion, exactly as with any other alteration of articles

options.D: The company must first obtain the approval of the stock exchanges on which its securities are listed, and no other governmental approval is required at any stage

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Such alteration (conversion into a private company) shall not take effect except with the approval of the Central Government (delegated to the Regional Director), applied for within 60 days of the special resolution, along with the prescribed documents

question_html: Within how many days of incorporation must a company (other than a specified IFSC company) have a registered office capable of receiving and acknowledging communications, and what is the general penalty for default under section 12?

options.A: Within 180 days of incorporation; on default, the company alone is liable to a fixed penalty of Rs. 10 lakh, with no separate liability imposed on any officer of the company
options.B: Within 30 days of incorporation; on default, the company and every officer in default is liable to a penalty of Rs. 1,000 for every day during which the default continues, subject to a maximum of Rs. 1 lakh
options.C: Within 15 days of incorporation; on default, the Registrar is empowered to immediately and compulsorily wind up the company, with no lesser penalty being available
options.D: Within 60 days of incorporation for every type of company without exception; on default, only the managing director (and no other officer) is liable to any penalty

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Within 30 days of incorporation; on default, the company and every officer in default is liable to a penalty of Rs. 1,000 for every day during which the default continues, subject to a maximum of Rs. 1 lakh

Section 12(1) requires a company to have a registered office within 30 days of incorporation (60 days for specified IFSC companies), verified to the Registrar within that period. Section 12(8) prescribes a penalty of Rs. 1,000 per day of continuing default, for both the company and every officer in default, subject to a maximum of Rs. 1 lakh.

question_html: Under section 10A, within what period must a company having a share capital, incorporated after the commencement of the Companies (Amendment) Ordinance, 2019, file a declaration confirming that subscribers have paid for their shares, and what may the Registrar do if this is not filed?

options.A: Within 30 days of incorporation, with no requirement of any professional verification; if not filed, the company is automatically and immediately dissolved without any further inquiry by the Registrar
options.B: Within 1 year of incorporation, verified solely by the managing director; if not filed, the Registrar must refer the matter directly to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal for adjudication
options.C: Within 180 days of incorporation, verified by a company secretary/chartered accountant/cost accountant in practice; if not filed within 180 days and the Registrar has reasonable cause to believe the company is not carrying on any business or operations, he may initiate action for removal of the company's name from the register
options.D: There is no fixed time limit for filing such a declaration, and the Registrar has no power to remove the company's name from the register even in the absence of such filing

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Within 180 days of incorporation, verified by a company secretary/chartered accountant/cost accountant in practice; if not filed within 180 days and the Registrar has reasonable cause to believe the company is not carrying on any business or operations, he may initiate action for removal of the company's name from the register

Section 10A requires a company (having share capital, incorporated after the 2019 Ordinance) to file a declaration (Form INC-20A, verified by a CS/CA/CMA in practice) within 180 days of incorporation, confirming subscribers have paid for their subscribed shares and that the registered office requirement under section 12(2) is satisfied. If not filed within 180 days, and the Registrar has reasonable cause to believe the company is not carrying on business, he may initiate action to remove the company's name from the register under section 248.

question_html: What is the effect of a company already registered under the Act converting itself into a company of another class, by altering its memorandum and articles?

options.A: The company is treated as an entirely new legal entity distinct from its pre-conversion self, so all its pre-conversion debts and liabilities are automatically extinguished and cease to be enforceable
options.B: Conversion under section 18 is not legally permitted under the Companies Act, 2013, and any company seeking to change its class must first be wound up and then re-incorporated afresh
options.C: The Registrar's fresh certificate of incorporation operates retrospectively from the date of the company's original incorporation, treating the company as though it had always been of the new class
options.D: The Registrar closes the former registration and issues a fresh certificate of incorporation after being satisfied that the requirements have been complied with, but such conversion does not affect any debts, liabilities, obligations, or contracts incurred or entered into by, with, or on behalf of the company before conversion - these remain enforceable as if the conversion had not taken place

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The Registrar closes the former registration and issues a fresh certificate of incorporation after being satisfied that the requirements have been complied with, but such conversion does not affect any debts, liabilities, obligations, or contracts incurred or entered into by, with, or on behalf of the company before conversion - these remain enforceable as if the conversion had not taken place

Section 18 permits a registered company to convert into another class by altering its memorandum and articles. The Registrar, on being satisfied of compliance, closes the former registration and issues a fresh certificate of incorporation. Critically, such conversion does not affect any pre-conversion debts, liabilities, obligations or contracts - the company remains the same legal entity for these purposes, and they continue to be enforceable as if the conversion had not taken place.

question_html: Which of the following is a recognised exception to the general prohibition under section 19 against a subsidiary company holding shares in its holding company?

options.A: Where the subsidiary holds shares in the holding company as the legal representative of a deceased member of the holding company
options.B: Where the subsidiary holds shares in the holding company through a nominee appointed specifically to circumvent the general prohibition, provided the nomination is disclosed to the Registrar
options.C: Where the subsidiary holds shares in the holding company for the purpose of exercising full voting rights at the holding company's annual general meeting
options.D: Where the holding company has given its express prior written consent for the subsidiary to acquire and hold shares in it, regardless of the capacity in which such shares are held

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Where the subsidiary holds shares in the holding company as the legal representative of a deceased member of the holding company

Section 19 prohibits a subsidiary from holding shares in its holding company (including through a nominee), and any allotment or transfer of shares in contravention is void. The recognised exceptions are: (i) where the subsidiary holds shares as the legal representative of a deceased member of the holding company, (ii) where it holds shares as a trustee, and (iii) where it was already a shareholder of the holding company before becoming its subsidiary - though in this last case, it has no right to vote at meetings of the holding company (except as a legal representative or trustee).

question_html: Which of the following is a mode of service of documents on a company or an officer of a company recognised under section 20?

options.A: Publishing the document as a public notice in at least two newspapers circulating in the district where the registered office is situated, without any direct communication to the company
options.B: Sending the document by registered post, speed post, or courier to the registered office of the company
options.C: Announcing the contents of the document at a press conference convened by the person seeking to effect service
options.D: Affixing the document to a public noticeboard maintained by the local municipal authority in the district of the company's registered office

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Sending the document by registered post, speed post, or courier to the registered office of the company

Section 20 recognises service of documents on a company/officer by sending it by registered post, speed post, courier, leaving it at the registered office, or by electronic or other prescribed mode. Can Coral Furnishings Limited avoid liability on the cheque merely because the signatory had, unknown to Naveen Traders, already been removed from the post of Finance Manager?

options.A: No - under the doctrine of indoor management, Naveen Traders, dealing in good faith and without notice of the internal change, was entitled to presume that the person held the position and internal authority he was represented to hold; the company remains bound
options.B: Yes, since the doctrine of constructive notice deems every outsider to have notice of all internal personnel changes within the company

The doctrine of indoor management (Turquand's Rule) protects an outsider, such as Naveen Traders, who deals in good faith without notice of an internal irregularity (here, the officer's removal) and is entitled to presume that the company's internal requirements/authorisations remain as represented. The company cannot escape liability by relying on its own unpublicised internal change.
